about.intro: Elevate Access Solutions provides practical, personalized accessibility and assistive technology solutions for individuals and organizations. We help people identify, learn, and use technology in ways that support confidence, independence, inclusion, and everyday access.
about.mission: Our mission is to help people use accessible technology with greater confidence and independence. We focus on practical access, inclusive participation, and solutions that support real needs in daily life, education, and work.
about.approach: Our services are individualized, goal based, and practical. Recommendations are informed by professional knowledge and lived experience, with attention to the person, task, workplace, educational setting, or daily environment where the technology will actually be used.

services.title: Assessments
services.description: Our comprehensive access technology assessments identify the tools, features, and training strategies that best support each individual’s goals. We evaluate current skills, technology needs, work or educational demands, and accessibility preferences to develop clear, practical recommendations. Each assessment is designed to help clients, families, educators, employers, and rehabilitation professionals make informed decisions about assistive technology, training, and long-term support.
services.summary: Clear recommendations informed by your skills, goals, technology needs, and everyday environment.

services.title: Assistive Technology Training
services.description: Our assistive technology training helps individuals build the skills and confidence needed to use accessible technology effectively in everyday life, education, and employment. Training is personalized to each client’s goals and may include screen readers, magnification tools, smartphones, computers, braille displays, productivity software, and other accessibility solutions. Sessions are practical, hands-on, and paced to support lasting independence.
services.summary: Practical, personalized instruction in screen readers, magnification, mobile accessibility, braille technology, and productivity tools.

services.title: Workplace Accessibility Consulting
services.description: Our workplace accessibility consulting services help organizations create more effective, inclusive, and sustainable work environments. We evaluate employee workflows, digital tools, and common workplace tasks to identify practical adjustments that improve visual comfort, efficiency, and performance. Recommendations may include display and contrast settings, text-size modifications, glare reduction, alternative software features, and targeted employee training. Each solution is designed to integrate smoothly into existing systems while supporting productivity, retention, and employee well-being.
services.summary: Accessible workflows, digital tools, and practical adjustments that support inclusion and productivity at work.

founders.name: Juanita Herrera
paragraphs: I am the co-founder of Elevate Access Solutions and have 15 years of experience working in the blindness field, including the past 12 years specializing in assistive technology. Throughout my career, I have provided personalized training on a wide range of assistive technology, helping individuals who are blind or have low vision develop the skills and confidence to succeed at home, in school, and in the workplace.

I have been a RESNA-certified Assistive Technology Professional since 2023, reflecting my commitment to maintaining high standards of knowledge, service, and professional practice. I have worked with children, adults, seniors, and professionals from a variety of backgrounds, combining technical expertise with my own perspective as a person who is blind.
I am passionate about helping others build confidence, increase their independence, and develop the practical skills they need to achieve their personal, educational, and professional goals.

portrait.alt: Juanita Herrera smiling in a black blazer.

founders.name: Fernando Macias
paragraphs: I am the co-founder of Elevate Access Solutions and have seven years of experience working with people with disabilities, with a particular focus on blindness, low vision, and assistive technology. Throughout my career, I have provided individualized and group training to help people use accessible technology more effectively at home, in education, and in the workplace.

My experience includes working with screen readers, magnification tools, mobile accessibility features, braille technology, productivity software, and other solutions that support greater independence. I have also conducted assistive technology assessments, developed training programs, and presented on accessibility and emerging technology to clients, professionals, and community organizations.

As someone who is blind, I bring both professional knowledge and lived experience to my work. I understand that effective technology training is not simply about learning commands or features—it is about finding practical solutions that fit the individual, build confidence, and support meaningful personal and professional goals.

portrait.alt: Fernando Macias wearing a navy suit and blue patterned tie.

articles.title: Can AI Agents Give People With Disabilities More Control Online?
articles.seo_title: AI Agents and Disability Access | Elevate Access Solutions
articles.description: How AI agents could make complex online tasks easier to direct and review
articles.author: Elevate Access Solutions
articles.image_alt: Illustrated traveler uses a phone while pulling a suitcase along tactile paving inside an airport terminal.
articles.body_html:
A blind traveler should be able to direct an online task, inspect the result, and decide when to seek help. Airline service-animal paperwork shows both the promise of AI agents and the work required to make that promise real.

Before a flight with a guide dog, a traveler may have to find the airline’s current instructions, locate the right form, gather veterinary and training details, enter them in a usable format, and complete a separate submission process. The difficulty is often the chain of steps, rather than any single question on the form.

An AI agent could prepare the routine parts and bring the work back for review. The traveler would still decide what information to provide, confirm personal attestations, and authorize submission. The test is whether that control remains usable throughout the process.

What an AI agent can do

An AI agent uses a model and software tools to work toward a goal across several steps. It can search, work with files, use a browser, inspect what happened, and adjust its next action. Anthropic distinguishes this flexible behavior from a workflow that follows a predefined path. [1]

That makes a practical difference. An assistant can explain the fields on a form; an agent with suitable access can locate the form, prepare entries from supplied records, and return a draft for the traveler to inspect. Its permissions and the design of the website determine how far the work can go.

Three agents worth examining

Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, and Grok Bot illustrate this emerging category. The descriptions below come from provider documentation checked October 10, 2026. We did not test these products on airline paperwork or independently assess their accessibility.

Muse

Meta describes Muse as a personal agent with its own virtual computer and browser. It can work across connected apps, continue a task in the background, and handle examples that include appointments and forms. The user can inspect its activity, manage permissions, and approve certain actions. Meta offers limited free use and paid options. [2]

Dots

OpenAI describes Dots as agents that continue work between conversations using a cloud computer, browser, and permitted tools. Users can inspect progress and intervene when a decision needs them. Dots are rolling out to eligible Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise accounts; access depends on plan, region, age, and workspace settings. [3]

Grok Bot

Grok Bot runs persistent Bots across apps and websites. Its documentation says Bots within one account share a cloud computer, files, browser sessions, and app logins. That arrangement makes permission boundaries especially important when different Bots handle different jobs. Access is available through eligible paid Cursor plans or linked individual SuperGrok subscriptions. [4]

ProductDocumented approachA question to test
Muse [2]Personal agent with a browser and connected appsCan I review a prepared form and approve actions accessibly?
Dots [3]Persistent work through a cloud computer and permitted toolsCan I access sign-in requests, results, and any required takeover?
Grok Bot [4] [5]Bots working across tools on a shared account computerCan I supervise the task and limit access to the relevant records?

Putting an agent to work on the airline form

For flights to, within, and from the United States, airlines may require the DOT Service Animal Air Transportation Form, which covers a dog’s health, training, and behavior. A separate relief attestation may be required on flights of eight hours or more. The rules apply to service dogs supporting people with a range of disabilities, including guide dogs. [6]

DOT says an airline that requires its form must provide an accessible format. Its sample PDF may work poorly in some browser viewers, so DOT recommends Adobe Acrobat Reader and encourages accessible HTML forms. The airline’s submission system adds another interface the traveler may have to navigate. [7]

Here is a useful division of work: the traveler names the airline and supplies the necessary records; the agent finds current instructions, drafts factual entries, flags missing information, and returns a field-by-field review. The traveler checks the entries, makes personal attestations, signs, and decides whether to authorize any supported submission step.

InformationAgent preparesTraveler decides
Handler and dog detailsDrafts entries from information suppliedChecks names, contact details, and description
Health and training recordsCopies relevant facts and flags gapsConfirms entries against the records
Attestations and submissionStops and presents a reviewable resultMakes attestations, signs, and authorizes submission

Figure 1. Preparing and reviewing a service-animal form.

The DOT form asks for handler details, a description of the dog, veterinarian and trainer contacts, and the rabies vaccination expiration date. The traveler submits the completed form to the airline. DOT also says airlines must assist a person who states that a disability prevents them from completing the form. [8]

A traveler might instruct an agent: “Find my airline’s current service-animal form and submission instructions. Prepare factual entries using only the records I provide. Ask about missing information. Give me a field-by-field review, and stop before signing, making attestations, or submitting.”

A completed form is not an accepted form. The traveler needs to know whether the agent drafted it, submitted it, or received confirmation from the airline—and see the document or confirmation that supports each status.

A different role for visual interpreting

A visual interpreter can help with an inaccessible form, a confusing layout, or an online submission. Aira describes human visual interpreting for tasks that include forms. If an agent produces a sound draft, a traveler could ask an interpreter to focus on the parts that need visual verification. [9]

That check has several levels. An interpreter might confirm that the text appears in the intended fields and is not cut off. With permission to view source records, they might compare a transcribed date or name against the original. The traveler remains responsible for personal attestations and chooses whether to sign and submit.

StepInterpreter throughoutAgent with targeted review
Gather informationTraveler and interpreter work togetherTraveler provides records to the agent
Enter detailsInterpreter assists with fields as neededAgent drafts entries for the traveler to inspect
Review and authorizeTraveler directs checks and submissionTraveler directs focused human checks, then decides

Figure 2. Two ways a traveler might organize assistance.

These are different checks: seeing a vaccination date in a field confirms its presence; comparing it with a veterinary record tests whether it was copied correctly. The reviewer can describe what the evidence shows without claiming to verify facts beyond it.

Aira already combines AI and human support in visual interpreting. Its Access AI descriptions can be checked by a human interpreter, while its Project Astra-powered AI Visual Interpreter tester program offers human verification or takeover. These services address visual information; they do not complete the airline workflow described here. [9] [10]

Focused review could help someone use available interpreting time more effectively. Whether it saves time or money depends on the entire job: preparation, corrections, failed attempts, human review, and any agent subscription. That outcome needs a real-world test.

Where else this could help

People need different ways to interact with technology. W3C documents barriers involving vision, movement, hearing, cognition, speech, stamina, and concentration. A useful agent must fit the person’s way of working. [11]

Someone with limited dexterity might delegate repeated data entry. Someone managing fatigue might have an agent gather records and prepare work asynchronously. Another person might ask for the missing information and decisions to be presented one at a time. Each use should be judged by the person who would rely on it.

Screen readers, magnification, speech recognition, switches, and other assistive technologies remain essential. Voice interaction can help, provided the same controls and results are available through accessible text and other input methods. [12]

What the research shows

Savant, a prototype described in a 2024 ASSETS paper, translated natural-language requests into sequences of screen-reader actions. In a study with 11 blind participants, researchers reported better efficiency and usability than the practices they compared it with. [13]

A 2026 CHI study followed 16 blind and low-vision programmers using AI coding assistance. The researchers found gains in efficiency and accessibility alongside difficulties expressing intent, interpreting output, and keeping track of work across multiple views. [14]

The studies show why this approach merits attention and why oversight matters. They studied a research prototype and programming work, respectively, rather than the three consumer agents or an airline submission.

The person must be able to supervise

A browser-capable agent is useful only if its owner can manage it. Setup, permissions, sign-in, progress reports, approval requests, results, and error recovery all need accessible controls. A takeover request that strands a blind traveler in an inaccessible browser defeats the purpose.

Grok Bot advises setting clear action boundaries and handling passwords and verification codes personally. OpenAI describes approval checks and steps that users must sometimes take over. Those controls need to work with the user’s assistive technology, not merely exist on a settings page. [3] [5]

A practical trial would give the agent access only to the records needed for one task, request a reviewable draft, and check key entries against the sources. It would count setup and verification as part of the work. Websites and documents must remain accessible in their own right so people can choose to complete the task directly.

The measure of independence

The measure is whether the traveler can follow the work and direct what happens next. Can they find out what the agent completed, correct a mistake, ask for a human review, and stop or authorize submission without losing access to the process?

Agents could remove some of the administrative work around travel and other services. Their value will be demonstrated in real tasks, when people with disabilities can use the controls themselves and trust the evidence of what was done.
